barometer: quantity or observation — Atmospheric pressure.

anemometer: quantity or observation — Wind speed.

rain gauge: working principle — Precipitation is collected over a known area.

seismograph: working principle — An inertial mass records ground motion.
ammeter: quantity or observation — Electric current.
ammeter: working principle — A low-resistance meter is connected in series.
voltmeter: quantity or observation — Potential difference.
voltmeter: working principle — A high-resistance meter is connected in parallel.

galvanometer: working principle — A current-carrying coil experiences magnetic torque.
potentiometer: quantity or observation — Electromotive force by comparison.
potentiometer: working principle — A null balance compares potential drops.
electroscope: quantity or observation — Presence of electric charge.
electroscope: working principle — Like charges repel movable leaves.
hydrometer: quantity or observation — Relative density of liquids.
hydrometer: working principle — Floating depth follows Archimedes' principle.
lactometer: quantity or observation — Relative density of milk.
lactometer: working principle — Buoyant floating depth changes with density.
manometer: quantity or observation — Pressure difference.
manometer: working principle — The height difference of a liquid column balances pressure.
speedometer: quantity or observation — Instantaneous vehicle speed.
speedometer: working principle — Wheel or shaft rotation is converted to a speed reading.
odometer: quantity or observation — Distance travelled.
odometer: working principle — Accumulated wheel rotations measure distance.
tachometer: quantity or observation — Rotational speed.
tachometer: working principle — The rate of shaft rotation is counted.
calorimeter: quantity or observation — Heat transferred.
calorimeter: working principle — An insulated system's temperature change indicates heat.
spectrometer: quantity or observation — Properties of a spectrum.
spectrometer: working principle — Light is separated according to wavelength.
microscope: quantity or observation — Magnified view of small objects.
microscope: working principle — Lenses or electron beams form an enlarged image.
telescope: quantity or observation — View of distant objects.
telescope: working principle — A large objective collects light from distant sources.
periscope: quantity or observation — View around an obstruction.
periscope: working principle — Successive reflections redirect the line of sight.
sonar: quantity or observation — Underwater distance or object location.
sonar: working principle — Echoes of sound reveal distance and direction.
radar: quantity or observation — Position or speed of distant objects.
radar: working principle — Reflected radio waves reveal target information.

EEG machine: working principle — Scalp electrodes record neural electrical signals.
spirometer: quantity or observation — Volumes of air breathed.
spirometer: working principle — Displaced air or airflow is integrated into volume.

stethoscope: quantity or observation — Internal body sounds.
stethoscope: working principle — Sound from the chest is conducted to the ears.
refractometer: quantity or observation — Refractive index.
refractometer: working principle — Refraction is related to the optical density of a sample.
polarimeter: quantity or observation — Rotation of plane-polarised light.
polarimeter: working principle — Optically active substances rotate the plane of polarisation.
photometer: quantity or observation — Light intensity.
photometer: working principle — A calibrated detector responds to light.

pyrometer: working principle — Thermal radiation is used to estimate temperature.

questions.explanation: Metal rails expand when heated so expansion allowances reduce buckling.

questions.question: At what temperature is pure water most dense near ordinary pressure?
questions.explanation: Water reaches maximum density close to 4°C.

questions.question: Why does ice float on liquid water?
options: Ice is denser than every liquid
Ice is less dense than liquid water
questions.explanation: The open crystal structure of ice occupies more volume for the same mass.

questions.question: Which law states that energy cannot be created or destroyed?
questions.explanation: The first law expresses conservation of energy for thermodynamic systems.

questions.question: What happens to temperature during melting of a pure substance at constant pressure?
options: It remains constant until melting is complete
questions.explanation: Added heat during melting supplies latent heat while solid and liquid coexist.

questions.question: Why is water kept in an earthen pot often cool?
options: The pot blocks all molecular motion
questions.explanation: Water evaporating from the porous wall takes latent heat from the remaining water.

questions.question: What is thermal equilibrium?
options: Bodies in contact have no net heat transfer because their temperatures are equal
questions.explanation: Temperature equality is the condition for thermal equilibrium.

questions.question: Which gas law relates volume inversely to pressure at fixed temperature for a fixed amount of gas?
questions.explanation: At constant temperature an ideal gas obeys PV = constant.

questions.question: Which gas law relates volume directly to absolute temperature at constant pressure?
questions.explanation: At fixed pressure and amount of gas volume is proportional to kelvin temperature.

questions.question: Which phenomenon explains the apparent bending of a pencil partly immersed in water?
questions.explanation: Light changes direction when it passes between media with different refractive indices.

questions.question: Why is the daytime sky blue?
options: The ocean reflects only blue light into space
Shorter visible wavelengths are scattered more strongly by air molecules
Air emits blue light because it is hot
Red light cannot enter the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Rayleigh scattering is stronger at shorter wavelengths.

questions.question: Why does the Sun appear reddish near sunset?
options: The atmosphere contains no particles at sunset
Red light travels slower only at night
The Sun's surface suddenly cools to room temperature
Much of the shorter-wavelength light is scattered out along the long atmospheric path
questions.explanation: The longer atmospheric path preferentially removes blue light from the direct beam.

questions.question: Which mirror is commonly used as a vehicle rear-view mirror?
options: Plane mirror with zero field of view
questions.explanation: A convex mirror forms an upright diminished image and provides a wide field of view.

questions.question: Which mirror can form an enlarged upright image of a nearby face?
questions.explanation: A concave mirror gives a virtual magnified image when the object is within its focal length.

questions.question: Which lens corrects simple myopia?
questions.explanation: A concave lens diverges incoming light so the image forms on the retina.

questions.question: Which lens corrects simple hypermetropia?
questions.explanation: A convex lens provides additional convergence for near vision.

questions.question: What causes dispersion in a glass prism?
options: Different wavelengths have different refractive indices in glass
questions.explanation: The refractive index varies with wavelength so colours emerge at different angles.

questions.question: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Red lies at the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum.

questions.question: Which visible colour has the highest frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency increases as wavelength decreases in a given medium.

questions.question: Why can sound not travel through a perfect vacuum?
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical disturbance carried by interacting particles.

questions.question: What determines the pitch of a sound?
questions.explanation: Higher frequency is perceived as higher pitch.

questions.question: What is most directly related to loudness for a given frequency?
questions.explanation: Greater amplitude generally gives greater intensity and perceived loudness.

questions.question: What is an echo?
options: A separately heard reflection of sound
questions.explanation: Reflected sound is heard separately when its delay is large enough.

questions.question: What is ultrasound?
options: Sound above the normal upper human hearing frequency
questions.explanation: Ultrasound has frequency above about 20 kHz.

questions.question: What is infrasound?
questions.explanation: Infrasound lies below the usual lower limit of human hearing.

questions.question: Which phenomenon changes the observed frequency when source and observer move relatively?
questions.explanation: Relative motion changes the rate at which wave crests reach the observer.

questions.question: Why do stars appear to twinkle?
options: Rapid changes in their actual size
Earth's magnetic field switches on and off
questions.explanation: Fluctuating air layers vary the apparent brightness and position of distant point sources.

questions.question: Which optical effect is used in optical fibres?
questions.explanation: Repeated total internal reflection confines light to the fibre core.

questions.question: What is the power of a lens measured in?
questions.explanation: Lens power in dioptres equals the reciprocal of focal length in metres.

questions.question: Which phenomenon creates a rainbow through raindrops?
questions.explanation: Raindrops refract and disperse sunlight with internal reflection producing the visible arc.

questions.question: Which wave can be polarised?
options: A longitudinal sound wave in air
A pressure wave in a fluid only
questions.explanation: Polarisation restricts the orientation of transverse oscillations.

questions.question: What does the focal length of a converging lens describe?
options: Distance from optical centre to principal focus for parallel rays
questions.explanation: Parallel paraxial rays converge at the principal focus.

questions.question: What kind of image does a plane mirror form?
questions.explanation: A plane mirror forms an equal-sized virtual image at equal distance behind it.

questions.question: What happens to light speed on entering ordinary glass from air?
questions.explanation: The refractive index of glass exceeds that of air.

questions.question: What remains unchanged when light passes from air into glass?
questions.explanation: The source fixes frequency while speed and wavelength change with the medium.

questions.question: Which unit is commonly used for sound level?
questions.explanation: The decibel expresses a logarithmic ratio such as sound intensity level.

questions.question: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum is used by a TV remote control?
questions.explanation: Most conventional remote controls send coded infrared pulses.

questions.question: Which electromagnetic radiation has the highest photon energy among these?
questions.explanation: Photon energy is proportional to frequency.

questions.question: Which colour of light is least deviated by an ordinary glass prism?
questions.explanation: Ordinary glass generally refracts longer visible wavelengths less strongly.

questions.question: What is diffraction?
options: Spreading of waves around edges or through apertures
Conversion of matter to sound only
questions.explanation: Diffraction is prominent when an opening is comparable to the wavelength.

questions.question: What is interference?
options: The creation of matter from nothing
questions.explanation: Overlapping coherent waves combine according to their relative phase.

questions.question: What causes a mirage above a hot road?
options: A pool of water must be present
The road emits visible water vapour
Refraction through air layers of different temperatures
questions.explanation: Strong temperature gradients bend light and can produce apparent reflections.

questions.question: Which radiation is commonly used for medical images of bones?
questions.explanation: Bone absorbs X-rays more strongly than surrounding soft tissue.

questions.question: Why are danger signals commonly red?
options: Red light is scattered relatively little by fog and air compared with shorter visible wavelengths
Red travels faster than all other colours in vacuum
questions.explanation: Longer visible wavelengths suffer less Rayleigh scattering.

questions.question: What is electric current?
options: Rate of flow of electric charge
questions.explanation: Current is charge transferred per unit time.

questions.question: What does Ohm's law state for a conductor at constant physical conditions?
options: Potential difference is proportional to current
questions.explanation: Ohm's law is V = IR for an ohmic conductor under fixed conditions.

questions.question: How are household appliances normally connected to the mains?
questions.explanation: Parallel branches receive the same supply voltage and can be switched independently.

questions.question: Why is a fuse placed in an electrical circuit?
options: To convert AC into light only
To melt and interrupt excessive current
questions.explanation: Heating at excessive current melts the fuse element and breaks the circuit.

questions.question: Which wire is connected to the metal body of a safely earthed appliance?
options: Neutral wire used as a switch
questions.explanation: Earthing provides a low-resistance fault path and helps protective devices operate.

questions.question: What energy conversion occurs in an electric motor?
questions.explanation: A motor uses magnetic forces to produce mechanical motion from electrical energy.

questions.question: What energy conversion occurs in an electric generator?
questions.explanation: A generator uses electromagnetic induction to convert mechanical input into electrical output.

questions.question: Which device changes AC voltage using electromagnetic induction?
questions.explanation: A transformer uses changing magnetic flux linking primary and secondary coils.

questions.question: Why does a simple transformer require changing current?
options: Steady flux always induces unlimited emf
Changing magnetic flux induces the secondary emf
questions.explanation: Faraday's law relates induced emf to the rate of change of magnetic flux.

questions.question: What happens to resistance of a uniform wire if its length doubles at the same cross-sectional area?
questions.explanation: Resistance is proportional to length for fixed material area and temperature.

questions.question: What happens to resistance if the cross-sectional area doubles at fixed length?
questions.explanation: Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area.

questions.question: What is the commercial electricity unit called one unit equivalent to?
questions.explanation: A kilowatt-hour is the energy used by a 1 kW load operating for one hour.

questions.question: What is the value of 1 kilowatt-hour in joules?
questions.explanation: One kilowatt-hour equals 1000 watts multiplied by 3600 seconds.

questions.question: Which effect of current is used in an electric heater?
questions.explanation: Electrical resistance converts electrical energy into thermal energy.

questions.question: Why is tungsten used in incandescent lamp filaments?
options: It has a very high melting point
It is a liquid at room temperature
questions.explanation: Tungsten tolerates the high temperature required for visible thermal radiation.

questions.question: What happens when like magnetic poles are brought together?
questions.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

questions.question: Where are the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet directed outside it?
options: From south pole towards north pole
From north pole towards south pole
questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines emerge from north and enter south outside the magnet.

questions.question: Which material is strongly attracted by a magnet?
options: Aluminium foil under all static conditions
questions.explanation: Iron is ferromagnetic and can be strongly magnetised.

questions.question: What does a capacitor primarily store?
options: Separated electric charge and electric-field energy
questions.explanation: A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between separated charges.

questions.question: Which device allows current mainly in one direction?
questions.explanation: A semiconductor diode conducts strongly in its forward direction and weakly in reverse under normal conditions.

questions.question: What is the main function of a transistor in many circuits?
questions.explanation: A transistor controls current and is used as an amplifier or switch.

questions.question: Which semiconductor is widely used in integrated circuits?
questions.explanation: Silicon's controllable electrical properties make it suitable for microelectronics.

questions.question: What is produced when light falls on a solar photovoltaic cell?
questions.explanation: Photovoltaic cells convert absorbed light energy into electrical energy.

questions.question: What is alternating current?
options: Current that can never change direction
A current existing only in batteries
questions.explanation: AC reverses direction periodically and commonly varies in magnitude.

questions.question: What is direct current?
options: Current flowing in a single direction
A current reversing direction every instant
questions.explanation: DC has a unidirectional flow though its magnitude can vary.

questions.question: Which factor can increase an electromagnet's strength?
options: Replacing the core with a perfect vacuum in every case
questions.explanation: More ampere-turns generally increase the magnetic field until magnetic limitations matter.

questions.question: Which instrument should be connected in series to measure a branch current?
questions.explanation: The branch current must pass through the ammeter.

questions.question: What is a short circuit?
options: An unintended low-resistance connection causing excessive current
questions.explanation: A low-resistance fault can draw dangerously large current.

questions.question: What is the equivalent resistance of two equal resistors R connected in series?
questions.explanation: Series resistances add because the same current flows through both.

questions.question: What is the equivalent resistance of two equal resistors R connected in parallel?
questions.explanation: The reciprocals of parallel resistances add.

questions.question: Which form of energy is released by nuclear fission?
options: Energy from a pressure difference alone
Energy from splitting a heavy nucleus
questions.explanation: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei and releases energy and neutrons.

questions.question: Which reaction is the principal source of the Sun's energy?
questions.explanation: Fusion converts light nuclei into heavier nuclei and releases binding energy.

questions.question: Which fuel is renewable on human timescales?
questions.explanation: Biomass can be replenished through biological growth when managed sustainably.

questions.question: Which energy source directly uses tides?
questions.explanation: Tidal power extracts energy from periodic sea-level changes or tidal currents.

questions.question: Which energy source draws on heat within Earth?
questions.explanation: Geothermal systems use heat from Earth's interior.

questions.question: What is a half-life?
options: Time for all atoms to disappear
Time for the atomic number to double
Time for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay
Time for a sample to melt
questions.explanation: After each half-life half of the previously remaining undecayed nuclei remain.

questions.question: Which radiation is stopped most easily by a sheet of paper?
questions.explanation: Alpha particles have low penetration despite strong ionising ability.

questions.question: What is beta-minus radiation?
options: Emission of an electron from a nuclear transformation
questions.explanation: In beta-minus decay a neutron transforms into a proton with electron and antineutrino emission.

questions.question: What are gamma rays?
options: High-energy electromagnetic radiation from nuclear transitions
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are photons rather than massive charged particles.

questions.question: Why should spent batteries be collected for safe recycling?
options: They can be safely burnt anywhere
They may contain hazardous substances and recoverable materials
questions.explanation: Controlled recycling reduces contamination and recovers useful resources.

questions.question: What distinguishes an element from a compound?
options: An element contains only one kind of atom
An element must be a gas
A compound has no fixed composition
questions.explanation: An element is defined by a single atomic number whereas a compound combines elements chemically.

questions.question: Which particle determines an element's atomic number?
questions.explanation: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus.

questions.question: What are isotopes?
options: Atoms of one element with different neutron numbers
Atoms with identical mass but different proton numbers only
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same proton number but different mass numbers.

questions.question: What are isobars?
options: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
questions.explanation: Isobars share mass number but have different atomic numbers.

questions.question: Which type of bond forms through transfer of electrons?
questions.explanation: Electron transfer creates oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction.

questions.question: Which type of bond involves sharing electron pairs?
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds arise through sharing electron pairs between atoms.

questions.question: What is the pH of a neutral aqueous solution at 25°C?
questions.explanation: At 25°C neutral water has equal hydrogen-ion and hydroxide-ion concentrations with pH 7.

questions.question: What happens to blue litmus in an acidic solution?
questions.explanation: Acids turn blue litmus red.

questions.question: What happens to red litmus in a basic solution?
questions.explanation: Bases turn red litmus blue.

questions.question: Which products usually form when an acid reacts with a carbonate?
questions.explanation: Acid–carbonate reactions release carbon dioxide in addition to salt and water.

questions.question: What is neutralisation?
options: Conversion of every atom to a neutron
Reaction of acid and base to form salt and usually water
questions.explanation: Neutralisation consumes acidic and basic species.

questions.question: Why does iron rust in moist air?
options: It reacts with oxygen and water
questions.explanation: Rust is hydrated iron oxide formed through oxidation in the presence of moisture.

questions.question: How does galvanising protect iron?
options: A zinc coating provides a barrier and sacrificial protection
It removes all oxygen from Earth
questions.explanation: Zinc corrodes preferentially and helps protect the underlying iron.

questions.question: Which alloy is mainly copper and zinc?
questions.explanation: Brass is chiefly an alloy of copper and zinc.

questions.question: Which alloy is mainly copper and tin?
questions.explanation: Traditional bronze consists mainly of copper with tin.

questions.question: Which element is added to steel to improve corrosion resistance in stainless steel?
questions.explanation: Chromium forms a protective oxide film on stainless steel.

questions.question: What is solder traditionally used for?
options: Joining metal parts using a lower-melting alloy
questions.explanation: Solder melts below the joined metals and forms an electrical or mechanical joint.

questions.question: Which allotrope of carbon is a good electrical conductor?
questions.explanation: Graphite has mobile electrons within its layered structure.

questions.question: Which allotrope of carbon is exceptionally hard?
questions.explanation: Diamond's three-dimensional covalent network gives it great hardness.

questions.question: Which carbon allotrope is a one-atom-thick sheet with a hexagonal lattice?
questions.explanation: Graphene consists of a single layer of sp²-bonded carbon atoms.

questions.question: What is a catalyst?
options: A substance that changes reaction rate without net consumption
Any material that changes atomic numbers
A product that contains no atoms
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway and is regenerated overall.

questions.question: What is oxidation in terms of electron transfer?
questions.explanation: Oxidation is electron loss; reduction is electron gain.

questions.question: What is reduction in terms of electron transfer?
questions.explanation: Reduction is electron gain by the species concerned.

questions.question: What does electrolysis use to drive a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous chemical reaction.

questions.question: Which process is used to separate components of crude oil?
questions.explanation: Fractions separate because they have different boiling ranges.

questions.question: Which technique separates insoluble solid particles from a liquid?
questions.explanation: A filter retains particles while allowing the liquid to pass.

questions.question: Which technique obtains a dissolved nonvolatile solid from its solution?
options: Decanting an unchanged clear solution only
questions.explanation: Removing solvent can leave the solute and controlled crystallisation improves purity.

questions.question: What is sublimation?
options: A liquid turning into two metals
Direct conversion between solid and vapour
questions.explanation: Some solids pass directly into vapour under suitable conditions.

questions.question: Which mixture shows the Tyndall effect?
options: A perfectly clear true solution in the ideal case
questions.explanation: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light and make its path visible.

questions.question: What is an emulsion?
options: A dispersion of one liquid in another immiscible liquid
questions.explanation: Milk is a familiar example of an emulsion.

questions.question: Why does soap clean oily dirt?
options: Its molecules help disperse oil into micelles in water
It converts all oil into oxygen
questions.explanation: Soap molecules have water-attracting heads and oil-attracting tails.

questions.question: Why is soap less effective in hard water?
options: Calcium and magnesium ions form insoluble soap scum
questions.explanation: Insoluble calcium and magnesium salts consume soap and reduce lather.

questions.question: Which salts mainly cause temporary hardness of water?
questions.explanation: Heating can decompose bicarbonates and remove much temporary hardness.

questions.question: Which treatment removes many disease-causing microbes from drinking water?
questions.explanation: Chlorination disinfects water when the dose and contact time are appropriate.

questions.question: What is an exothermic reaction?
options: A reaction that releases heat to its surroundings
A reaction that absorbs heat only
A reaction with no energy change by definition
questions.explanation: Exothermic processes transfer heat out of the reacting system.

questions.question: What is an endothermic process?
options: A process that releases heat only
A process that absorbs heat from surroundings
questions.explanation: Endothermic processes require heat input from their surroundings.

questions.question: Which gas is usually released when a reactive metal reacts with a dilute nonoxidising acid?
questions.explanation: Many metals displace hydrogen from dilute acids and form a salt.

questions.question: Which gas relights a glowing splint?
questions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion and can relight a glowing splint.

questions.question: Which gas turns clear limewater milky?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide produces insoluble calcium carbonate in limewater.

questions.question: Why is nitrogen used in some food packages?
options: It acts as an unlimited source of oxygen
Its relative inertness helps reduce oxidation
It is a strong acid in the packet
questions.explanation: Replacing oxygen with nitrogen slows many oxidative changes.

questions.question: What does LPG used for cooking mainly contain?
questions.explanation: Liquefied petroleum gas is chiefly a mixture of propane and butane.

questions.question: What is the main component of CNG?
questions.explanation: Compressed natural gas consists mainly of methane.

questions.question: Which pollutant interferes with oxygen transport by binding strongly to haemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide forms carboxyhaemoglobin and reduces oxygen delivery.

questions.question: What is a polymer?
options: A mixture that has no molecules
A large molecule formed from repeating smaller units
questions.explanation: Monomers join to form polymer chains or networks.

questions.question: Which material is a natural polymer?
questions.explanation: Cellulose is built from glucose units in plant cell walls.

questions.question: Which synthetic polymer is used in nonstick coatings?
questions.explanation: Polytetrafluoroethylene is commonly known by the trade name Teflon.

questions.question: What does vulcanisation improve in natural rubber?
options: Strength elasticity and durability through cross-linking
questions.explanation: Sulphur cross-links rubber chains and improves practical properties.

questions.question: Which metal is liquid near ordinary room temperature?
questions.explanation: Mercury melts below ordinary room temperature and is liquid under common conditions.

questions.question: Which nonmetal is liquid near ordinary room temperature?
questions.explanation: Bromine is a reddish-brown liquid at ordinary room temperature.

questions.question: What is the role of cryolite in aluminium extraction?
options: It supplies all oxygen in air
It lowers the effective melting temperature and improves conductivity of the electrolyte
It replaces aluminium atoms with iron
questions.explanation: Alumina dissolved in molten cryolite can be electrolysed at a more practical temperature.

questions.question: Which process enriches an ore by removing lighter gangue with water?
questions.explanation: Hydraulic washing exploits density differences between ore and gangue.

questions.question: Which method is particularly useful for concentrating sulphide ores?
questions.explanation: Differences in wetting allow sulphide particles to attach to air bubbles.

questions.question: What is an amphoteric oxide?
options: An oxide that cannot form salts
An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases
questions.explanation: Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are common amphoteric oxides.

questions.question: Which oxide is generally acidic?
questions.explanation: Many nonmetal oxides form acids or react with bases.

questions.question: Which oxide is generally basic?
questions.explanation: Metal oxides such as calcium oxide commonly react with acids to form salts.

questions.question: Which scale describes acidity in aqueous solutions?
questions.explanation: The pH scale is based on hydrogen-ion activity.

questions.question: What is a saturated solution at a specified temperature?
options: A solution with no dissolved matter
A solution holding as much dissolved solute as equilibrium permits
questions.explanation: Further solute does not dissolve at equilibrium unless conditions change.

questions.question: What is distillation based on?
questions.explanation: Distillation separates substances by volatility and collects condensed vapour.

questions.question: What does chromatography exploit to separate substances?
options: Different affinities for mobile and stationary phases
questions.explanation: Components move at different rates because their interactions with the two phases differ.

questions.question: What is a suspension?
options: A heterogeneous mixture with particles that can settle
A true solution with molecular-size particles only
questions.explanation: Suspended particles are large enough to settle or be filtered in many cases.

questions.question: What is the basic structural and functional unit of life?
questions.explanation: Cells are the smallest units capable of the basic processes of life.

questions.question: Which cell structure controls movement of substances into and out of a cell?
questions.explanation: The selectively permeable plasma membrane regulates exchange with the surroundings.

questions.question: Which cell structure contains enzymes for intracellular digestion?
questions.explanation: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that break down cellular materials.

questions.question: Which organelle modifies sorts and packages many cellular products?
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus processes and directs proteins and lipids.

questions.question: What gives plant cell walls much of their strength?
questions.explanation: Cellulose microfibrils strengthen plant cell walls.

questions.question: Which material is characteristic of fungal cell walls?
questions.explanation: Chitin is a major structural component of many fungal cell walls.

questions.question: Which cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus?
questions.explanation: Bacteria and archaea have genetic material without a membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.question: What is osmosis?
options: Only movement of solids by gravity
Movement of protons into a nucleus
Net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane down its water-potential gradient
questions.explanation: Osmosis is water movement through a selectively permeable membrane.

questions.question: What is diffusion?
options: Net movement of particles down a concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Random molecular motion gives net movement from higher to lower concentration.

questions.question: What distinguishes active transport from simple diffusion?
options: It requires no membrane proteins in every case
It can move substances against a gradient using energy
questions.explanation: Active transport couples energy use to uphill transport.

questions.question: What is the genetic material in most living organisms?
questions.explanation: DNA stores hereditary instructions in its nucleotide sequence.

questions.question: Which base is present in RNA but normally absent from DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil where DNA normally uses thymine.

questions.question: Which sugar is present in DNA?
questions.explanation: DNA nucleotides contain deoxyribose sugar.

questions.question: Which base pairs with adenine in DNA?
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with thymine through hydrogen bonding in normal DNA.

questions.question: Which base pairs with guanine in DNA?
questions.explanation: Guanine and cytosine form a complementary base pair.

questions.question: What is a gene?
options: A hereditary DNA sequence with a functional product or role
questions.explanation: Genes carry information used to make functional RNA or proteins.

questions.question: Where are genes arranged in eukaryotic cells?
questions.explanation: Chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins and carry genes.

questions.question: How many chromosomes are normally present in a human somatic cell?
questions.explanation: Most human somatic cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes.

questions.question: How many chromosomes normally occur in a human gamete?
questions.explanation: Meiosis produces haploid gametes with one chromosome from each pair.

questions.question: Which division halves chromosome number to form gametes?
questions.explanation: Meiosis reduces chromosome number and promotes genetic variation.

questions.question: Which cell division usually produces two genetically similar daughter cells for growth?
questions.explanation: Mitosis preserves chromosome number in ordinary growth and repair.

questions.question: What is fertilisation?
options: Fusion of male and female gametes
Splitting of one cell without fusion
Transfer of pollen to a stigma only
questions.explanation: Fertilisation combines genetic material from the two gametes.

questions.question: What is a zygote?
options: The cell formed by fusion of gametes
questions.explanation: The zygote is the first diploid cell of a new sexually produced organism.

questions.question: What is pollination?
options: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
questions.explanation: Pollination precedes fertilisation in flowering plants.

questions.question: Which organism commonly reproduces by budding?
questions.explanation: A bud grows from the parent and may separate as a new Hydra.

questions.question: Which process is typical of Amoeba reproduction?
questions.explanation: Amoeba commonly divides into two daughter cells.

questions.question: What is a dominant allele in a simple Mendelian cross?
options: An allele expressed in a heterozygote
An allele always most common in nature
An allele found only in males
questions.explanation: Dominance describes expression in a heterozygote rather than population frequency.

questions.question: What is a recessive allele in a simple Mendelian trait?
options: An allele masked by a dominant allele in a heterozygote
An allele present only in mitochondria
questions.explanation: A recessive allele is expressed in the absence of a dominant counterpart in the simple model.

questions.question: Who established classic inheritance ratios using pea plants?
questions.explanation: Mendel's pea experiments revealed basic patterns of inheritance.

questions.question: What is a mutation?
options: Only a change in body temperature
questions.explanation: Mutations alter DNA sequence or chromosome structure or number.

questions.question: What does genotype describe?
questions.explanation: Genotype refers to the alleles or genetic makeup considered.

questions.question: What does phenotype describe?
options: Observable characteristics produced by genes and environment
questions.explanation: Phenotype includes observable traits influenced by genotype and environment.

questions.question: Which sex-chromosome combination is typical of a human male?
questions.explanation: Most human males have one X and one Y chromosome.

questions.question: Which gamete normally determines chromosomal sex in humans?
questions.explanation: Sperm can contribute X or Y whereas an ovum normally contributes X.

questions.question: What is natural selection?
options: Change of all traits by need alone
A deliberate choice by every organism
Differential survival and reproduction of heritable variants
questions.explanation: Heritable variants affecting reproductive success can change in frequency over generations.

questions.question: What are homologous organs?
options: Structures with common evolutionary origin that may have different functions
Structures with identical function but no shared origin by definition
questions.explanation: The vertebrate forelimb is a classic example of common ancestry with modified function.

questions.question: What are analogous structures?
options: Structures with similar function arising independently
Structures always inherited unchanged from one recent common ancestor
questions.explanation: Bird and insect wings illustrate similar function with different evolutionary origins.

questions.question: What is a fossil?
options: Preserved remains or traces of past life
questions.explanation: Fossils provide evidence about organisms and environments of the past.

questions.question: What is vaccination designed to produce?
options: Immune memory against a pathogen or its components
questions.explanation: Vaccines train adaptive immunity and can reduce future disease risk.

questions.question: What do antibiotics primarily target?
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act against bacterial processes and do not treat viral infections directly.

questions.question: Which enzyme begins digestion of starch in the mouth?
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase starts breaking down starch.

questions.question: Which enzyme digests proteins in the acidic stomach?
questions.explanation: Pepsin works in the stomach's acidic environment.

questions.question: What is the main digestive role of bile?
options: Digesting DNA directly by a bile enzyme
questions.explanation: Bile salts disperse fats into small droplets and aid lipid digestion and absorption.

questions.question: Which blood vessels normally carry blood away from the heart?
questions.explanation: Arteries are defined by flow away from the heart rather than oxygen content.

questions.question: Which vessels normally carry blood towards the heart?
questions.explanation: Veins return blood towards the heart.

questions.question: Which blood vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

questions.question: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from lungs to heart?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

questions.question: How many chambers are present in a normal human heart?
questions.explanation: The human heart has two atria and two ventricles.

questions.question: Which chamber pumps blood into the aorta?
questions.explanation: The muscular left ventricle supplies the systemic circulation.

questions.question: Which blood group is often called the universal red-cell donor in emergencies?
questions.explanation: O-negative red cells lack A B and Rh D antigens though compatibility testing remains important.

questions.question: Which ABO blood group has both A and B antigens on red cells?
questions.explanation: AB red cells carry both A and B antigens.

questions.question: Which pigment gives human red blood cells their red colour?
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin contains haem groups and carries much of the blood's oxygen.

questions.question: Which hormone lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and storage?
options: Adrenaline in its main acute effect
questions.explanation: Insulin helps cells take up glucose and favours glycogen synthesis.

questions.question: Which pancreatic hormone raises blood glucose during fasting?
questions.explanation: Glucagon promotes glucose release from liver stores and new glucose production.

questions.question: Which hormone is commonly associated with the fight-or-flight response?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline rapidly increases cardiovascular and metabolic readiness during stress.

questions.question: Which hormone helps regulate the sleep–wake cycle?
questions.explanation: The pineal gland secretes melatonin in a rhythm linked to darkness.

questions.question: Which hormone promotes water reabsorption by the kidneys?
questions.explanation: ADH increases water conservation by the kidney.

questions.question: Which hormone stimulates uterine contractions during childbirth?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin supports uterine contraction and milk ejection.

questions.question: Which nitrogenous waste is the main product excreted by adult humans?
options: Uric acid as the sole waste
Ammonia as the main circulating waste
questions.explanation: The liver converts toxic ammonia into urea for renal excretion.

questions.question: Which structures carry urine from kidneys to urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: Each ureter conveys urine from a kidney to the bladder.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of dialysis in severe renal failure?
options: Removing wastes and excess fluid from blood
questions.explanation: Dialysis substitutes for important filtration functions of failing kidneys.

questions.question: Which response is an example of a reflex action?
options: Rapid withdrawal from a painful stimulus
questions.explanation: Reflexes are rapid automatic responses through neural circuits.

questions.question: Which nervous-system division generally prepares the body for stress?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic activation supports the fight-or-flight response.

questions.question: What is homeostasis?
options: Maintenance of relatively stable internal conditions
Change of all genes at once
questions.explanation: Feedback systems regulate variables such as temperature and blood glucose.

questions.question: Which body protein is abundant in hair and nails?
questions.explanation: Keratin is a tough structural protein of hair nails and the outer skin.

questions.question: Which protein is abundant in connective tissue such as tendons?
questions.explanation: Collagen fibres provide tensile strength in connective tissues.

questions.question: What is pasteurisation?
options: Controlled heating to reduce harmful microbes in food or drink
questions.explanation: Pasteurisation uses a validated time–temperature treatment without necessarily sterilising the product.

questions.question: What is the principal immediate danger of severe diarrhoea?
questions.explanation: Loss of fluid and salts can be life-threatening if not replaced.

questions.question: Why does oral rehydration solution contain glucose and salts?
options: The solution replaces antibiotics in every disease
Salt removes all bacteria from the blood
Glucose-assisted sodium absorption helps water uptake
questions.explanation: Sodium–glucose cotransport promotes intestinal fluid absorption.

questions.question: What does BMI compare?
questions.explanation: Body mass index is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared.

questions.question: Which nutrient yields the most energy per gram among these?
options: Dietary fibre counted as fully digestible glucose
questions.explanation: Fat provides about 9 kcal per gram while protein and digestible carbohydrate provide about 4.

questions.question: Which dietary component supplies essential amino acids?
questions.explanation: Proteins are digested into amino acids including those the body cannot make in sufficient amounts.

questions.question: What is an ecosystem?
options: Only the animals in a zoo
Organisms interacting with one another and their physical surroundings
questions.explanation: An ecosystem includes biotic and abiotic components and their interactions.

questions.question: Which organisms form the first trophic level of a typical grazing food chain?
questions.explanation: Producers convert external energy into organic matter.

questions.question: What is the role of decomposers?
options: Breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients
questions.explanation: Decomposers return nutrients to ecosystems.

questions.question: What does the usual ten-percent rule describe approximately?
options: Exact salt concentration in every ocean
Energy transfer between successive trophic levels
The fraction of Earth made of gold
The number of genes in every cell
questions.explanation: Only a limited fraction of energy at one trophic level becomes biomass at the next.

questions.question: What is biomagnification?
options: Increase of all nutrients in rainwater
Increasing concentration of some persistent substances at higher trophic levels
Reduction of every pollutant through food chains
questions.explanation: Persistent bioaccumulating pollutants can become more concentrated up a food chain.

questions.question: What is eutrophication?
options: Nutrient enrichment that can cause algal growth and oxygen depletion
questions.explanation: Excess nutrients stimulate growth and subsequent decomposition can reduce dissolved oxygen.

questions.question: Which gas is fixed by Rhizobium in legume nodules?
questions.explanation: Rhizobium converts atmospheric nitrogen into biologically usable compounds.

questions.question: Which process returns nitrogen gas to the atmosphere from nitrates?
questions.explanation: Denitrifying microbes reduce oxidised nitrogen compounds to nitrogen gases.

questions.question: What is biodiversity?
options: Variety of life at genetic species and ecosystem levels
questions.explanation: Biodiversity includes variation within species among species and across ecosystems.

questions.question: What is in-situ conservation?
options: Moving every animal to a laboratory
Protecting species in their natural habitats
Keeping all species only in museums
questions.explanation: Protected natural habitats support in-situ conservation.

questions.question: What is ex-situ conservation?
options: The complete removal of genetic material
Protection only in an undisturbed forest
questions.explanation: Zoos botanical gardens and seed banks are examples of ex-situ measures.

questions.question: Which atmospheric layer contains the ozone maximum that shields much ultraviolet radiation?
questions.explanation: Stratospheric ozone absorbs much harmful ultraviolet radiation.

questions.question: Which chemicals were major contributors to ozone depletion?
questions.explanation: CFC-derived chlorine can catalytically destroy stratospheric ozone.

questions.question: Which process removes carbon dioxide from air into plant biomass?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis fixes carbon dioxide into organic compounds.

questions.question: Why can deforestation worsen erosion?
options: Roots and vegetation cover no longer protect the soil
questions.explanation: Vegetation stabilises soil and reduces the erosive impact of water and wind.

questions.question: What is a nonbiodegradable waste example?
questions.explanation: Conventional polyethylene persists because biological breakdown is extremely slow.

questions.question: What is an indicator species?
options: A species whose presence absence or condition reveals environmental conditions
Any species chosen at random without information
questions.explanation: Indicator species can provide clues about ecosystem quality or change.

questions.question: What does biological oxygen demand indicate?
options: The speed of sound in water
The mass of all fish scales
Oxygen needed by microbes to decompose biodegradable matter in water
questions.explanation: High BOD often signals organic pollution and risk of oxygen depletion.

questions.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Mercury has the smallest mean orbital distance from the Sun.

questions.question: Which planet is the largest in the Solar System?
questions.explanation: Jupiter has the greatest planetary mass and diameter in the Solar System.

questions.question: Which planet is famous for its extensive bright ring system?
questions.explanation: Saturn's conspicuous rings are composed largely of icy particles.

questions.question: Which planet has a very dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere and extreme surface heat?
questions.explanation: Venus's dense atmosphere causes a strong greenhouse effect.

questions.question: What causes the phases of the Moon?
options: The Moon producing varying nuclear energy
Changes in the Moon's actual shape
Changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth
Earth's shadow falling on it every night
questions.explanation: The geometry of Sun Earth and Moon changes the visible illuminated fraction.

questions.question: What happens during a solar eclipse?
options: The Moon comes between Sun and Earth
Earth comes between Sun and Moon
questions.explanation: The Moon's shadow can fall on Earth during a solar eclipse.

questions.question: What happens during a lunar eclipse?
options: The Moon comes between Sun and Earth
Earth comes between Sun and Moon
questions.explanation: The Moon passes through Earth's shadow.

questions.question: What mainly causes Earth's seasons?
options: Only the distance from Earth to Sun
Monthly changes in the Moon's colour
Axial tilt combined with Earth's revolution around the Sun
questions.explanation: Axial tilt changes solar angle and day length through the year.

questions.question: Which movement mainly causes day and night?
questions.explanation: Earth turns so different regions face towards and away from the Sun.

questions.question: What is the main reason for ocean tides?
options: Wind as the sole universal cause
Differential gravitational effects of the Moon and Sun
questions.explanation: Lunar and solar gravitational gradients produce tidal effects.

questions.question: What is a geostationary satellite?
options: A satellite in a circular equatorial prograde orbit with Earth's rotational period
Any satellite passing over the poles
A satellite fixed above a pole without propulsion
Any object outside the Solar System
questions.explanation: Its orbital motion matches Earth's rotation so it appears fixed above one longitude.

questions.question: What does remote sensing obtain?
options: Information about a target without direct physical contact
questions.explanation: Sensors on satellites or aircraft measure reflected or emitted signals.

questions.question: What does GPS primarily provide?
questions.explanation: GPS derives position and time from signals transmitted by navigation satellites.

questions.question: What is a black hole?
options: A star with no gravitational field
An empty hole in Earth's crust
A region whose event horizon prevents light from escaping
A cold cloud made only of oxygen
questions.explanation: A black hole's gravity creates an event horizon beyond which outward light cannot escape.

questions.question: What powers a main-sequence star like the Sun?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen fusion in the core supplies the energy of main-sequence stars.

questions.question: What is a galaxy?
options: A gravitationally bound system of stars gas dust and dark matter
A small cloud in Earth's atmosphere
questions.explanation: The Milky Way is the galaxy containing the Solar System.

questions.question: What is an asteroid?
options: A small rocky or metallic body orbiting the Sun
questions.explanation: Many asteroids orbit in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.

questions.question: What commonly produces a comet's tail near the Sun?
options: The comet transforms into a planet
The comet burns atmospheric oxygen in space
questions.explanation: Solar heating drives sublimation and releases material shaped by radiation and solar wind.

questions.question: What is a meteor?
options: A luminous atmospheric phenomenon caused by an incoming meteoroid
Any rock resting on the ground
questions.explanation: A meteoroid heats the atmosphere and itself while entering at high speed.

questions.question: What is a meteorite?
options: Material from space that reaches Earth's surface
Only a comet still orbiting the Sun
questions.explanation: A surviving fragment of a meteoroid is called a meteorite.

questions.question: Which layer of Earth lies between crust and core?
questions.explanation: The mantle is the thick silicate layer beneath the crust.

questions.question: Which type of rock forms from cooling magma or lava?
questions.explanation: Solidification of molten material produces igneous rocks.

questions.question: Which type of rock forms by heat and pressure altering existing rock?
questions.explanation: Metamorphism changes mineral assemblages and textures without complete melting.

questions.question: What is the focus of an earthquake?
options: The point within Earth where rupture begins
The point directly above the source on the surface
questions.explanation: The focus or hypocentre is the subsurface origin of earthquake rupture.

questions.question: What is the epicentre of an earthquake?
options: The point on Earth's surface above the focus
Every location where shaking is felt
The deepest part of the outer core
questions.explanation: The epicentre is the surface projection of the hypocentre.

questions.question: What is a tsunami generally caused by?
options: Sudden displacement of a large volume of water
questions.explanation: Submarine earthquakes are a common cause of major tsunamis.

questions.question: What is the CPU's main role in a computer?
options: Storing all data permanently without power
Displaying images without any other component
questions.explanation: The central processing unit performs instruction execution and control.

questions.question: What is RAM primarily used for?
questions.explanation: RAM normally stores data and instructions currently in use and is usually volatile.

questions.question: Which storage type retains data without continuous power?
options: A CPU register as permanent storage
questions.explanation: Nonvolatile storage preserves data when power is removed.

questions.question: What is an operating system?
options: Software managing hardware resources and providing services to applications
questions.explanation: An operating system coordinates memory processes files and devices.

questions.question: What does a web browser do?
options: Provides all electricity to a computer
questions.explanation: Browsers interpret web resources and provide an interface for navigating them.

questions.question: What does HTTPS add to ordinary HTTP communication?
options: Transport encryption and server authentication through TLS
A guarantee that every webpage claim is true
questions.explanation: HTTPS protects transport confidentiality and integrity but does not certify content truth.

questions.question: What is phishing?
options: Deceptive communication intended to steal sensitive information
A way to increase battery capacity
questions.explanation: Phishing often impersonates trusted organisations to obtain credentials or money.

questions.question: Why is multifactor authentication useful?
options: It makes passwords visible to everyone
It requires more than one type of verification
questions.explanation: Independent verification factors reduce dependence on a password alone.

questions.question: What is a computer virus?
options: Malicious code that can replicate by infecting other files or programs
A biological microbe living in silicon
questions.explanation: Viruses spread by attaching to or modifying host files or programs.

questions.question: What is a backup?
options: A separate copy for recovery if original data is lost
questions.explanation: Backups support recovery from accidental loss corruption or device failure.

questions.question: What is encryption?
options: Deleting all information irreversibly by definition
Encoding information so authorised keys are needed to recover it
questions.explanation: Encryption protects data confidentiality through cryptographic transformation.

questions.question: What is machine learning?
options: A way to bypass all uncertainty
A machine having no input or rules
Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions
questions.explanation: Machine-learning systems fit models from examples or interaction data.

questions.question: What is a sensor?
options: A screw used solely for fastening
A device that detects a physical condition and produces a usable signal
questions.explanation: Sensors convert quantities such as light pressure or temperature into signals.

questions.question: What does 3D printing create?
options: Objects by adding material according to a digital model
questions.explanation: Additive manufacturing builds objects layer by layer or through other controlled deposition methods.

questions.question: What is biotechnology?
options: Use of biological systems or organisms for useful products or processes
questions.explanation: Biotechnology includes fermentation genetic engineering and many medical or agricultural applications.

questions.question: What is PCR used to do?
options: Remove every gene from a cell
questions.explanation: Polymerase chain reaction produces many copies of a target DNA region.

questions.question: What is an enzyme?
options: A gas used only in balloons
A biological catalyst usually made of protein
A metal that always melts in water
questions.explanation: Enzymes accelerate biochemical reactions with substrate specificity.

questions.question: What is fermentation by yeast commonly used to produce?
options: Ethanol and carbon dioxide from sugars
questions.explanation: Yeast can metabolise sugars anaerobically to ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.question: What is genetic engineering?
questions.explanation: Genetic engineering modifies DNA to introduce or change biological functions.

questions.question: What is nanotechnology concerned with?
options: Materials and devices at approximately nanometre scales
questions.explanation: At nanoscale dimensions materials can show distinctive physical and chemical properties.

questions.question: What is a rechargeable battery?
options: A cell whose chemical changes can be substantially reversed by charging
A cell that creates energy from nothing
A cell that can never be reused
questions.explanation: Secondary cells store energy through reversible electrochemical reactions.

questions.question: What is a fuel cell?
options: A device with no chemical reaction
A container that burns coal only to make steam
A device producing electricity electrochemically from continuously supplied fuel and oxidant
questions.explanation: Fuel cells convert chemical energy directly into electrical output.

questions.question: Why is electronic waste a resource as well as a pollution concern?
options: It contains recoverable metals and potentially hazardous components
It consists only of clean water
It is always safe to dump in rivers
questions.explanation: Controlled recycling can recover valuable materials while limiting harmful releases.

questions.question: What is carbon capture intended to do?
options: Separate carbon dioxide for use or storage
questions.explanation: Carbon capture reduces the amount of carbon dioxide reaching the atmosphere from targeted sources.

questions.explanation: Newton's second law gives F = ma = 2 × 3 = 6 N.

questions.explanation: Newton's second law gives F = ma = 4 × 2 = 8 N.

questions.question: A 100 W appliance runs for 2 hours. How much electrical energy does it use?
questions.explanation: Energy in kWh = power in kW × time in hours = 0.1 × 2 = 0.2 kWh.
